attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his newsletter, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: The claim keeps the attribution to tweet traffic and interviews and the overreaction framing. 'Jumped at their own shadow' is fairly paraphrased as overreacted. It is causal because it says the publicity moved the idea.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair and ordinary: Coxon's publicity materially brought slowdown proposals into broad international discussion. It does not require him to be the sole cause or a majority to agree. 'Global zeitgeist' has no measure, so the interpretation matters.

evidence.note: BBC Brasil, Sept 13–14. It shows the post went viral and reached an international audience. It also credits Amodei's slowdown essay and backing from Altman and Musk, which are competing causes. There is no baseline.
TechRadar, Sept 14. It shows the slowdown debate had international reach (China, Trump), but it centres on Amodei's essay. It has no before-and-after measure and does not isolate Coxon's effect.

reviews.rationale: Both items show that slowdown talk was circulating internationally by Sept 14. Neither gives the before-and-after measure the contract requires. Both also point to Amodei's essay and other CEOs' statements as drivers, so Coxon's share of the effect cannot be separated out. The packet confirms circulation but not that Coxon caused the shift.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence. The quoted 'heard a lot of my colleagues' phrase is his paraphrase of Coxon, used inside his own claim.

semantics.note: The claim keeps 'in many cases' and the 'even if' concession. The causal core is that the warnings scared a lot of people. 'Specious' is an evaluative judgement attached to that core.

contract.note: Treating 'specious' as a claim of thin evidentiary basis is a reasonable reading. The contract correctly says a single well-grounded warning does not refute 'in many cases'. Support requires both the fear part and the characterization of the warnings; that requirement drives the result.

evidence.note: WSJ syndication, Sept 17, before the evaluation date. It reports Coxon 'freaked out so many people so quickly', which supports the fear part. This is reporting, not a measured causal estimate.

Advocacy-group survey fielded the day after the warning. It shows concern and government-priority rises, not fear specifically. It notes the Hugging Face hack also moved opinion, so Coxon's effect is not isolated.

CBS interview. Coxon framed his dangers as future and conditional and called current AI safe to use. This bears on what 'things he's talking about' means but does not settle whether the warnings were specious.

OpenAI's own disclosure about itself. It documents real misaligned agent behavior behind the Hugging Face incident, a concrete basis for one warning. Under the qualifier, that rebuts only that one part.

reviews.rationale: News reporting (e1) and the survey's rise in concern (e2) back the claim that Coxon's warnings scared many people, though no source isolates his effect from the Hugging Face news. The packet neither proves nor disproves the 'specious in many cases' characterization: e4 grounds only one warning. The contract needs both parts for support, so the compound claim is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own factual assertion, made in his own voice.

semantics.note: The factual core matches. The drafter weakened 'next three years' to 'over three years' and dropped the list of compute providers. The 'worrying' judgement is evaluative and is rightly left unscored.

contract.note: Taking 'next three years' as Sept 2026 to Sept 2029 follows his words. Requiring a projection that covers that window, and refusing figures for a later endpoint, is a fair standard.

evidence.note: Yahoo, July 22, citing WSJ. It reports about $750B in projected compute spending through 2030, a longer horizon. That suggests the three-year share would be smaller, but the contract bars using a later endpoint, and the figure may have been updated by Sept 14.

reviews.rationale: The only usable source gives about $750B through 2030, not the three years he named. That implies the three-year share was likely under $750B, which is a real problem for the claim. But no projection with a matching schedule, current at Sept 14, is in the packet, and the contract forbids substituting the longer horizon. So the claim is neither confirmed nor cleanly refuted.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion. The phrases he quotes ('white collar bloodbath', 'LLMs blackmailing people') name the stories he is criticizing; they are not claims he is quoting from others.

semantics.note: The claim keeps all four strands he listed and the unqualified 'not based on anything LLMs can do'. It is a firm statement about the past, so observation is the right kind.

contract.note: 'Not based on anything' is categorical, so reading it as a blanket denial that any strand had a capability basis is fair. The contract also correctly avoids crediting Claude results to the unidentified GPT-4 story. Tracing 'stories about AI 2027' back to AI 2027's own analysis is reasonable, since those stories reported that analysis.

evidence.note: AI 2027's timelines forecast (April 2025) explicitly builds on METR's measured LLM task-horizon trend. That is a capability basis for that strand, whatever the merits of the extrapolation.
METR, March 2025. It supplies the measured capability data and also says agents cannot reliably replace workers. That confirms a basis exists and shows its limits.
Anthropic's 2025 simulated blackmail demo with Claude. It is not the early-GPT-4 story and not real-world blackmail, so under the contract it cannot settle that strand.

reviews.rationale: The claim says none of the named strands rested on anything LLMs can do. At least one strand, AI 2027, explicitly rests on measured LLM capabilities (METR's task-horizon data). That meets the contract's contradiction condition, even though the forecast's extrapolation is speculative. The other strands remain unsettled, but one counterexample defeats the blanket denial.
